Explanation: The core value unit is a merchant-controlled storefront: the products, prices, brand presentation and checkout experience that a shopper can browse and buy from using Shopify-powered commerce tools.
Shopify owns and operates the commerce platform that merchants use to build stores and run transactions across online, retail and other channels.
Shopify has to make it easier for merchants to start, operate and grow a business while keeping checkout and core commerce infrastructure reliable.
Shopify earns more when more merchants join and when existing merchants sell more and use additional merchant services.
Shopify must keep a global commerce system secure and reliable while supporting many merchant sizes, countries, channels, payment methods and third-party apps.
Shopify charges subscription fees and earns merchant-solution revenue from services such as payments, transaction-related services and other commerce tools.
Transaction Flows: ← Provider · Store / Fees — Merchants run their commerce business on Shopify and pay subscriptions and applicable service or transaction-related fees. | → Provider · Commerce Tools — Shopify provides the storefront technology, admin, checkout, payments, analytics and other tools merchants use to run commerce. | ← Partner · Apps / Extensions — Developers extend Shopify with apps and integrations that solve specialized merchant needs. | → Partner · APIs / Revenue — Shopify provides APIs, distribution through the App Store and revenue opportunities that let developers build businesses on the platform.

Explanation: Shopify sets the rules for merchants, payments, apps, APIs, security, data use and participation in its ecosystem.
Shopify grows through merchant referrals, agencies and partners, its own brand and products such as Shop that can help merchants reach buyers.
Shopify develops the commerce platform, runs checkout and payments infrastructure, supports merchants and maintains the APIs and ecosystem around the core product.
Key resources include the Shopify platform, checkout technology, Shopify Payments and Shop Pay, merchant data, APIs, developer tools and the merchant ecosystem.
People buy from independent brands and retailers whose stores are powered by Shopify. They may reach those stores directly, through social media, search, the Shop app or other sales channels.
Shoppers want to find a product they like, trust the store, pay easily and receive the order without needing to understand the technology behind the store.
They can buy directly from many different brands while using familiar checkout, payment and order-tracking experiences.
Because every merchant has its own store, shoppers can face different brands, policies, delivery options and levels of trust.
The shopper places an order with a merchant and pays through the store's checkout, which may use Shopify Payments and Shop Pay.
Transaction Flows: ← Provider · Store / Products — The merchant presents its own brand, products and storefront directly to shoppers rather than placing everything inside one central Shopify marketplace. | → Provider · Order / Payment — The shopper buys from the merchant. Shopify can power the checkout and payment experience, but the commercial relationship is with the merchant.

Explanation: Access depends on the merchant's market, product, shipping and payment rules, together with fraud and payment checks.
Shoppers normally enter through a merchant's own storefront, but Shopify can also support discovery and repeat purchasing through Shop and other connected channels.
They browse products, choose a merchant, complete checkout and track or manage their order.
Shoppers contribute attention, purchase intent, account or contact details, payment information and order history.
Businesses use Shopify to create and operate their own commerce experiences rather than listing everything inside one shared Shopify marketplace.
Merchants need to build a store, manage products and inventory, accept payments, fulfill orders and sell across different channels.
They keep their own brand and storefront while using shared technology for checkout, payments, operations, analytics and extensions.
Merchants still have to attract their own customers and manage marketing, margins, apps, fulfillment and the cost of running the store.
The merchant publishes products, accepts orders and is responsible for delivering the goods or services purchased by the shopper.

Explanation: Merchants choose a Shopify plan and must follow platform, payments, app and acceptable-use requirements.
The Shopify Admin is the main operating interface for products, orders, inventory, customers, analytics, apps and sales channels.
Merchants create the storefront, manage products and prices, market the brand, process orders and support customers.
They bring the products or services, brand, product content, inventory, customer relationships and fulfillment capability.
Independent developers build apps and extensions that add specialized functions to Shopify stores and merchant operations.
Developers fill specific merchant needs such as marketing, subscriptions, support, accounting, fulfillment, analytics and store design.
They can sell software and services to Shopify's large merchant base and build recurring businesses on top of the platform.
Developers depend on Shopify's APIs, review rules and platform changes while competing with many other apps and some native Shopify features.
Developers provide software, extensions and services that merchants can install or connect to their Shopify setup.

Explanation: Public apps must meet Shopify's technical, security, privacy and App Store requirements.
Developers use Shopify APIs, developer tools and the App Store to build, distribute and support integrations.
They build apps, maintain integrations, support merchants and adapt to changes in Shopify's platform.
They contribute software, industry knowledge, specialized functionality and support capacity that Shopify does not need to create internally.
